name: Hesperidin
short: Case reports: DRESS, a severe drug reaction, after diosmin with hesperidin. A related form, glucosyl hesperidin, showed no clinically relevant blood test changes in human studies (EFSA).
text: Safety data on hesperidin taken alone are limited in the cited sources. An EFSA panel opinion on glucosyl hesperidin (a related form made enzymatically from hesperidin and dextrin, for use in foods and supplements) noted that human intervention studies reported no clinically relevant changes in blood count or blood chemistry with doses of up to 3 g/day for 12 weeks, found no genotoxicity concern, and judged the product safe at the intakes it assessed (up to 364 mg per day for adults). In a meta-analysis of 47 randomised trials of 15 dietary polyphenols in rheumatoid arthritis, in which hesperidin was tested in only one trial, adding polyphenols did not increase adverse events; the abstract gives no hesperidin-specific figures. Case reports describe drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), a severe skin and systemic reaction for which one report gives a mortality rate of 3.8-10% (a figure for DRESS in general, not for hesperidin), after the combination of diosmin and hesperidin, not hesperidin alone; in one, a 34-year-old woman had markedly raised liver enzymes and, two months later, a relapse of the rash and raised liver enzymes with a positive herpes simplex IgM test, and she had also taken a systemic sunscreen product beforehand. In a rat study of a hesperidin isolate (73%) from orange peel, a single oral dose of 5000 mg/kg killed 10% of the animals; in a sub-chronic study, 250 and 500 mg/kg caused no abnormalities, while 1000 mg/kg altered body and organ weights, blood tests and tissue histology, and the authors judged the safety profile good (animal data). No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
